builder_plan.scenario: Your self-hosted model spends too long generating answers token by token.
builder_plan.change: Check whether a compatible draft model and serving integration exist before renting compute.
builder_plan.baseline: The same target with speculation off, then your existing drafter if you have one.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Accepted draft length, tokens per second, tail latency, output quality, and total GPU cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
summary: The method replaces full-width hidden-state draft models in speculative decoding (DFlash, EAGLE-3) with drafts whose residual stream runs at half or a quarter of the target's hidden width, folding the output adapter into the borrowed vocabulary projection so logits are unchanged up to rounding. The cost is training a new narrow draft per target model and accepting a small reduction in token acceptance, which the reported end-to-end speedups indicate is outweighed by cheaper draft passes. Adoption can fail if no trained draft exists for the reader's target model, if serving stacks do not yet expose this configuration, or if acceptance-rate degradation at the reader's temperature, domain, or batch regime erases the latency gain.
rationale: Speculative decoding is one of the few inference speedups a small team can adopt through SGLang or vLLM without training a model, and narrower drafts compound that gain at negligible integration risk, though the reader must first train or obtain a compatible draft for their specific target model.
technique: Narrow-width draft models for speculative decoding

claims.statement: The method replaces full-width hidden-state draft models in speculative decoding (DFlash, EAGLE-3) with drafts whose residual stream runs at half or a quarter of the target's hidden width, folding the output adapter into the borrowed vocabulary projection so logits are unchanged up to rounding. The cost is training a new narrow draft per target model and accepting a small reduction in token acceptance, which the reported end-to-end speedups indicate is outweighed by cheaper draft passes. Adoption can fail if no trained draft exists for the reader's target model, if serving stacks do not yet expose this configuration, or if acceptance-rate degradation at the reader's temperature, domain, or batch regime erases the latency gain.

Narrowing the speculative draft's residual stream to half or a quarter of the target's hidden width speeds end-to-end decoding by 1.06–1.12x on a B200 and 1.13–1.44x on a GB10 at batch 1 and temperature 0, with gains up to 1.21x at large batches and no narrow draft slower than full width.
